title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation. Our preregistered binary episode success required (a) validator acceptance of the final config, (b) no emulator-measured availability degradation above tolerance, and (c) no automatic rollback during execution. We completed 1,199 paired observations: baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0). The paired success–rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Provider audit shows shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair-stage calls = 3. Under the supplied synthetic corpus and validator configuration we observe no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline. Important caveats and limitations are documented, and all execution and analysis artifacts are archived. Note: the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown hypothesis (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup test; archived confirmatory artifacts contain only aggregated paired results (see Methods and Results).

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and system work emphasize that operational reliability depends on orchestration, deterministic validators, provenance, and sandboxed execution rather than on the base LLM alone [1,2]. A common mitigation architecture is generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted): the LLM proposes a candidate, an automated verifier enforces syntactic and semantic constraints, and an automated repair loop iterates until verifier rules are satisfied. Although generator+verifier patterns are widely advocated, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence that measures whether verifier assistance yields a reliably larger operational success rate (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is sparse.

We report NetOpsTraceBench (study_id = rX4f7-1), a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded evaluation that compares (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline using the same shared initial candidate for each pair. The research question was: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topology clusters? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered experimental design and frozen execution artifacts (rX4f7-1); (2) a confirmatory paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation (the confirmatory test used an exact McNemar test appropriate for paired binary outcomes) plus explicit documentation that the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and therefore remains untested in the archived confirmatory artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and systems work frame LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and stress that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the full orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandbox) rather than of the base LLM alone [1–3]. Multiple reviews call for workflow‑centered evaluation (trace quality, validator interactions, rollback‑aware metrics) rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests and motivate reproducible benchmarks that combine generation, deterministic validation, and emulation [1,2,4].

Concrete verifier‑assisted approaches appear across adjacent domains and NetOps prototypes: NL→formal translators use verifier loops to repair CTL/specification outputs; topology compilers enforce compliance constraints during intent→topology synthesis; LLM firewalls and prototype config‑generation systems use deterministic parsers and rule sets to accept/reject or trigger repairs [5–10]. Empirical analyses of LLM failure modes—hallucination, unit/semantic errors, miscalibration, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection—motivate guarded architectures but also highlight sensitivity to task design and verifier strictness [11–14]. NetOpsTraceBench operationalizes recommended workflow‑centered evaluation practices by preregistering inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, a binary rollback‑aware success metric, and by archiving raw outputs, validator traces, and execution manifests for reproducible interpretation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered (rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) and froze confirmatory hypotheses, inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination thresholds, seeds, stopping rules, and analysis plan before any model calls. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the preregistration targeted an absolute paired increase of 5 percentage points (MDE = 0.05) with α=0.05 and power=0.8 under assumed baseline ≈0.70.

Task corpus and pairing semantics: The benchmark defined 1,200 deterministic operator‑intent tasks split conceptually into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Each task was generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with frozen per‑task seeds. The execution contract used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task a single initial generation (shared_initial_candidate) was produced and supplied to both conditions to isolate verifier/repair effects from generation variability. Provider audit records show shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair calls = 3 (execution manifest). This design intentionally isolates the verifier's effect by holding the candidate constant across paired episodes; as a result, repair invocation frequency depends only on verifier rejections and repair policy rather than independent generation noise.

Paired conditions and validator: Baseline (one‑shot) recorded the shared initial candidate and proceeded to deterministic parsing and emulator preflight checks without invoking repair. Guarded (verifier‑assisted) validated the same shared candidate using deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation"); if rejected, a single automated repair iteration (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) could be invoked per preregistration. Validator traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, validation_before/after, and repair_applied flags.

Contamination, exclusions, and analysis executor: Contamination detection used conservative thresholds; pairs flagged for contamination or where both episodes failed to produce parsable configs after one automated re‑execution would be excluded deterministically (no human adjudication). The preregistration specified paired_binary_analysis_v1 for the primary test. Because outcomes are binary, the archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test on aggregated paired outcomes and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. The confirmatory analysis artifacts archived are analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, and analysis/results.json (these files contain only aggregated paired results; see the Results section). Important note required by peer review: the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup test; archived confirmatory artifacts contain only the aggregated paired analysis described above, and therefore H3 remains untested in the confirmatory archive.
sections.results:
Execution and pair accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199). Provider audit records hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 and stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3.

Primary aggregated confirmatory outcomes: The aggregated paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 1,196 (both succeeded), n10 = 3 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). From these counts baseline_success = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149 and guarded_success = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0000000000. The observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851.

Confirmatory inference and CI: The archived exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 on the discordant pairs (n10 = 3, n01 = 0). The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) for the paired difference is [0.0000, 0.0058381985]. The lower CI bound at zero and the small discordant count indicate limited resolution to detect effects much smaller than the preregistered MDE.

Missingness and repairs: Missingness artifacts report complete_pairs = 1,199 and two failed episodes (failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1). Contamination screening did not exclude pairs (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty). Repair invocation was rare: repair_stage calls = 3 and representative scoring artifacts show validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for the majority of episodes, indicating the shared initial candidate usually passed deterministic validation.

Topology‑cluster breakdown (preregistration H3) — explicit disclosure: The preregistration included H3 as a confirmatory hypothesis to test consistency of the paired effect across the two simulated topology clusters (edge vs core). The archived confirmatory analysis artifacts contain only the aggregated paired contingency table and condition summary and do not include per‑cluster contingency tables or inferential subgroup tests. Therefore H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and remains untested in the archived confirmatory outputs. The absence of confirmatory per‑cluster results is a documented deviation from the full preregistration; raw per‑task artifacts (task_manifest entries and per‑episode scoring JSONs) are archived and permit later exploratory or post‑hoc per‑cluster summaries, but such subgroup tests were not performed as part of the confirmatory analysis reported here (no new model calls or post‑hoc confirmatory testing were executed to satisfy H3). This explicit omission is included to satisfy reviewer requirements and to preserve a transparent record of which preregistered confirmatory tests were run.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The aggregated confirmatory analysis shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the supplied synthetic corpus and validator settings (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded explanations are supported by the archived evidence. First, near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%) left little headroom for absolute improvement; the preregistered MDE (5 percentage points) assumed a much lower baseline, so the run was underpowered to detect the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point effect. Second, the shared_initial_candidate design and the task/validator configuration materially reduced repair invocation: provider audit shows shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3, and representative validator traces show validation_after.valid = true for most episodes. Holding the initial candidate constant isolates verifier effects but, for these deterministic synthetic tasks, produced initial candidates that typically satisfied the verifier and therefore limited measurable gains from repair.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is strong because seeds, deterministic task generation, and automated exclusion rules were frozen. Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) maps to operationally meaningful correctness in production; emulator fidelity and the validator rule set are proxies and have limits. External validity is constrained: only one requested model family (gpt-5-mini) was exercised; tasks were synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic; and Mininet‑style emulation may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies, routing convergence, or production transient behaviors. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant pairs implies low power to detect small absolute effects; the observed null result should be interpreted in this bounded context.

Operational implications and next steps: When initial LLM outputs already satisfy deterministic verifier criteria on well‑specified synthetic tasks, generate–validate–repair will be rarely exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To assess verifier value in practice, future benchmarks should increase task ambiguity/adversarial content, vary verifier strictness, and exercise multiple LLM families and vendor renderers. The archived raw artifacts (per‑episode responses, validator traces, and task manifests) permit reproducible exploratory subgrouping and sensitivity studies without new model calls; such secondary analyses remain outside the reported confirmatory results to preserve preregistration integrity.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench produced a preregistered, artifact‑rich paired evaluation comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines. Under the supplied synthetic task corpus, deterministic validator settings, and gpt-5-mini as requested, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%). The guarded pipeline improved absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) but this small effect is not statistically significant under the archived confirmatory test (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Provider audit shows that repair was invoked only three times, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate design and validator acceptance rates. We explicitly disclose that the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis and therefore remains untested in the confirmatory archive; raw per‑task artifacts are archived to permit later exploratory per‑cluster summaries. The run and its artifacts are archived to enable reproducible follow‑up analyses and sensitivity studies that vary corpus difficulty and verifier strictness.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.

Preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup test; per‑cluster inferential results are absent from the confirmatory archive and remain untested in that confirmatory analysis.
